doc.title: Frank Tiberi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 30, 2022

title: Decline of big bands and colleges
summary: Tiberi says the college big-band circuit and old venues vanished, and bands like Herman's were canceled.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well as long as you mentioned that, maybe I’ll ask your opinion about the state of jazz in America at this point. We have hundreds of universities with fine jazz programs, of course you’re part of one of the major ones. But on the other end sales of recordings and live, the club scene, has changed a lot. Do you have any opinions about where jazz is at right now?

Well for the past two years I mean it’s obvious that things have really closed right on through. That’s the particular thing about even teaching jazz you know, where are they going to be playing and to what area would they be getting into? We at that time, when we were traveling and playing every night it was always colleges, it was always schools. Because they didn’t have any bands as they have right now actually. I mean in Berklee right now we have three bands that are operating. Now as I say but at that time, but not right now, that canceled us, the big bands. That was the thing that really right now canceled us, outside of the money that has to be paid for musicians.
Can I ask you to say that again? What was it that canceled you?
Maybe you were saying there was more of a market because the colleges did not yet have the bands of their own?

They didn’t have any bands actually. They didn’t have that much of a curriculum. And the high schools also as well, they might have had a few musicians you know but not jazz bands. So a lot of them, we got canceled pretty much when I mean who needs the Woody Herman band at Berklee right now, where — I don’t know. Or other bands actually. But I don’t know how Berklee hires the bands. I think they, I think most of the bands have to really support themselves. I think so, I don’t know.
Are you able or do you think it’s even relevant to teach students about the bandstand? About professionalism? About getting a gig and keeping it? Or is that not even as relevant anymore?

Well at first I mean there are not many bands that are operating right now. You know, like as there were before. The musicians would be going through just switching a lot of bands at that particular time. But you know you’re talking about all the places that you will be able to really play or be hired actually, all the venues such as the Earle Theater and the Atlantic City Steel Pier — all these things are not operating right now. These were the things which everybody looked forward to be able to go with the band. Like you’re talking about the 400 bands that were operating at that time. And then there were also local bands too also that were operating.
So all the students that graduate every year from the universities if they come and ask for your advice about making a living, do you have anything you can tell them these days?
